rationale: A wins because it does the grown-up PR thing: it names four real reporter-shaped paths and tells the founder what would kill each one before the pitch goes out. Its customer angle says, "Without one, this collapses into a product announcement in customer-story clothing," which is exactly the proof gate this launch needs. B has usable bones, but "Brex spends big on global infrastructure without saying if it's profitable" smuggles in a cost claim the update does not prove.
gaps_in_A: "Corporate Cards Were a US Startup Story. Now the Software Is Going Everywhere." overstates the supplied record; the update says Brex serves many venture-backed startups, not that the whole category was a US startup story.
"employee complaints about out-of-pocket costs" is plausible buyer pain, but it is not in the update and needs a customer before it belongs in outreach.
"historically been the incumbent advantage" is a useful thesis, but still needs comparison data against Ramp, Amex, Citi, or another issuer before it becomes pitchable.
gaps_in_B: "Brex spends big on global infrastructure" is too loaded; the facts give scope, not spend, burn, cost, or infrastructure investment.
"whoever proves global capability first" implies first-mover stakes the update never establishes.
"CFOs of global startups actually asked for" narrows "top enterprise customer request" into a CFO/startup claim without evidence.
Refusing a "traditional corporate-card issuers" angle as "duplicate" throws away a distinct incumbent-vs-fintech story that is explicitly in the update.
